# Draft:List of actors nominated for an Academy Award for playing multiple roles

----
According to the rules of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, a performer may receive only one acting nomination for a single film, regardless of the number of roles portrayed. The nomination is awarded for the overall performance, rather than for individual characters. Additionally, performers may not be nominated in more than one acting category for the same film. This rule was formalized in 1944 after Barry Fitzgerald received both Best Actor and Best Supporting Actor nominations for his performance in Going My Way (1944) at the 17th Academy Awards.
, 16 performers have been nominated for portraying two or more distinct characters within the same film. The first such case was Fredric March, who won for his performance of both Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde (1931). The first performance involving two separate characters was Charlie Chaplin, who received a best actor nomination for portraying both Adenoid Hynkel and a Jewish barber in The Great Dictator (1940). The most recent were the 2025 nominations of Michael B. Jordan for portraying the twin brothers in Sinners (2025) and and Wagner Moura for a father and son in The Secret Agent (2025). To date, 7 performers have won Academy Awards Fredric March, Joanne Woodward, Lee Marvin, Michelle Yeoh, Ke Huy Quan, Jamie Lee Curtis, and Emma Stone.
Most nominations have come in leading roles, with eight best actor nomination and two wins and four best actress nomination and three wins. The list excludes disguises, pseudonyms, aliases, stage names, noble titles or assumed identities, where the character is essentially the same individual, name changes, body possession or the like.

Criteria
For the purposes of this list, a performance is considered eligible if it meets at least one of the following conditions:
* Distinct individuals: The performer portrays two or more separate characters who coexist within the same narrative world and are treated by the film as independent persons, each with their own identity, agency, and narrative function (for example, twins, unrelated characters, or multiple historical figures).
* Narrative duality or multiplicity: The performer portrays two or more distinct consciousnesses, personalities, or identities occupying the same physical body, provided that the narrative treats them as separate entities rather than as a single evolving character.
* Metanarrative separation: The performer portrays two characters who exist on different narrative levels (for example, a fictional character and an actor portraying that character), as long as both are presented by the film as autonomous narrative agents rather than as a single dramatic role.
* Multiversal or alternate-reality variants: The performer portrays multiple versions of the same individual across parallel universes or timelines, provided that these versions are depicted as narratively autonomous characters with distinct life trajectories.
The following cases are not considered multiple roles for the purposes of this list: disguises, pseudonyms, aliases, stage names, noble titles or assumed identities, where the character remains ontologically the same individual; name changes without a corresponding change in narrative identity; psychological transformations (such as amnesia, breakdowns, or standard character development arcs); body possession or consciousness transfer when only one narrative identity remains active; performative transformations in which the character remains the same narrative entity; and symbolic, metaphorical, or thematic doubling not treated by the narrative as literal character multiplicity
